summary: Explains how telephone numbers in the E.164 format are used with the Session Initiation Protocol, and how ENUM, which maps phone numbers to internet addresses through DNS, fits in. It describes procedures and gives guidance for implementers who must handle phone numbers in SIP.

eli5.summary: Phone numbers and internet addresses are different kinds of names. This document is a guide to translate between them so calls can find their way.

subtitle: Connecting phone numbers and internet addresses for voice calls

tldr.problem: SIP and VoIP systems use internet addresses, but the phone network uses telephone numbers in E.164 format; there is no automatic way to connect a phone number to an internet destination.
tldr.mechanism: ENUM uses DNS to look up telephone numbers and return SIP URIs or other internet addresses. This RFC explains how SIP applications should use ENUM, how to write DNS records for phone-to-URI mapping, and what to do when ENUM is not available.
tldr.outcome: SIP applications can now reliably route calls from phone numbers by querying DNS, bridging the gap between the telephone network and the internet.

facts.label: Primary purpose
facts.value: Translate phone numbers to SIP URIs

today: RFC 3824 is an Informational RFC that remains current. ENUM and E.164 are widely used by VoIP carriers and SIP providers to route calls from phone numbers to internet destinations.

sections.title: The Problem: Phone Numbers and Internet Calls
sections.content:
SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) is the standard for initiating internet calls, instant messaging, and video. It uses URIs (like sip:alice@example.com) to identify destinations. However, many SIP users need to call people using traditional telephone numbers in E.164 format (like +12025332600).

The problem is that a telephone number contains no routing information. Unlike a SIP URI, you cannot look at a phone number and know where on the internet to send the call. ENUM solves this by using DNS to translate E.164 numbers into URIs that SIP can use.
sections.eli5: Imagine you have a phone number but you only know how to reach people on the internet. ENUM looks up the phone number in DNS (the internet's directory) and tells you the internet address you need.

sections.title: Key Concepts
sections.content:
E.164 is the ITU-T standard international numbering plan that assigns unique phone numbers to every phone worldwide. All globally reachable telephone numbers follow E.164 format.

ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping) is defined in RFC 3761 and uses the DNS NAPTR resource record to map E.164 numbers to URIs. NAPTR records are DNS records that can be processed according to rules specified by the DDDS (Dynamic Delegation Discovery System) algorithm.

Address-of-record is a SIP user's canonical identity (the address that appears in the From field of outgoing calls), while a contact address is the URI of a specific device. ENUM records should map to addresses-of-record, not devices.
sections.eli5: E.164 is the world standard for phone numbers. NAPTR records are special entries in the internet's phone book. ENUM uses them to look up phone numbers and find the right internet address.

sections.title: Design Principles for ENUM and SIP
sections.content:
There are four key principles for integrating ENUM with SIP: First, ENUM records should point to addresses-of-record (long-term identities), not contact addresses (temporary device locations), because DNS records persist longer than SIP device registrations. Second, SIP URIs in ENUM should not carry capability information; SIP has its own mechanisms for negotiating capabilities between endpoints.

Third, ideally only one SIP URI appears in an ENUM record set for a phone number. If a user has multiple contact addresses, it is more flexible to have a SIP location service (which may also be registered in ENUM) that manages those addresses. Fourth, user agents (client devices) should process ENUM records, not proxy servers, because proxies do not know which services the calling client supports.
sections.eli5: Keep ENUM records simple and long-term. Point to a person, not a phone. Let the person's SIP server handle the details of which device to ring. Let the calling program do the ENUM lookup, not the middleman.

sections.title: How to Use ENUM with SIP
sections.content:
When a SIP user agent has a phone number as its target, it constructs a DNS query using ENUM to look up the number in the e164.arpa domain. The response contains NAPTR records with a Service field of E2U+sip, indicating that the URI field contains a SIP address-of-record.

If multiple NAPTR records are returned, the client selects one based on preference values. The client then extracts the SIP URI from the regexp field of the NAPTR record and uses it as the Request-URI for the SIP call. If ENUM returns no records or is unavailable, the client can create a tel: URL or route the call through a PSTN gateway using local policy.
sections.eli5: The SIP client asks DNS: what is the SIP address for this phone number? DNS answers with NAPTR records. The client picks the best one and uses the SIP address it contains.

sections.title: Handling Multiple Records and Processing
sections.content:
If an ENUM query returns multiple NAPTR records with SIP services, a SIP user agent must select one to use as its Request-URI. The agent should choose the most-preferred record (using the preference field). If multiple records share the highest preference, the agent may choose randomly or apply local policy.

Proxy servers can also process ENUM, but with limitations: they can fork the request to multiple URIs, but they should build the route using only SIP URIs from NAPTR records. Alternatively, a proxy can select a single record and proxy the request. The RFC recommends that proxies act as redirect servers (returning multiple addresses to the client) rather than as forking proxies, to avoid the complexity of managing multiple outbound calls.
sections.eli5: When there are multiple ways to reach someone, pick the best one. If there is a tie, pick randomly or use a local rule. Let the calling program decide, not the middleman router.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
ENUM records are public in DNS; anyone can look up a phone number and learn the associated SIP URI. This means that if someone creates an ENUM entry mapping a phone number to a SIP address like julia.roberts@example.com, their name becomes discoverable. However, SIP itself can require authentication and authorization before alerting the user, providing greater protection against unwanted calls than the traditional phone system.

Users uncomfortable with revealing their name can publish less revealing SIP URIs, such as sip:anonymous00045@example.com or sip:anonymous00045@anonymous-redirector.example.org, which forwards to their real SIP address. DNSSEC can protect against DNS spoofing attacks on ENUM lookups.
sections.eli5: ENUM records are public, so your phone number might reveal your SIP address. But you can use a fake name. And unlike the old phone system, SIP can make you prove who you are before it rings your phone.
